summary: Describes a backward-compatible way to add new elements to the Geopriv civic address format used in location information. It also defines how unsupported extensions are handled when converting between XML and DHCP civic address forms, and defines some initial new elements.

eli5.summary: Addresses sometimes need new lines, like a building name. This lets forms add new lines without confusing programs that do not know about them.

questions: how to extend pidf-lo civic addresses
how to add new civic address elements
how are civic address extensions converted between dhcp and xml
what new civic address elements does rfc 6848 add
subtitle: How to add new fields to civic addresses without breaking old software, including when an address is converted between DHCP and XML.

tldr.problem: New fields keep being needed in civic addresses (street, house number and so on), but software that does not know a new field simply drops it, especially when an address is converted between the DHCP and XML formats.
tldr.mechanism: New elements are defined only in XML, in their own namespace. In the DHCP format they travel inside one generic extension CAtype (code 40) that carries the namespace, the element name and the value, so a converter needs no knowledge of the extension.
tldr.outcome: Extensions survive translation in both directions, numeric CAtype registration is closed, and four example elements are registered: pole number, milepost, street type prefix and house number prefix. It also updates RFC 5222 so LoST responses must qualify element names with a namespace.

today: RFC 6848 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2013. It updates RFC 4776 and RFC 5222, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Civic Addresses Need Extensions
sections.content:
The Geopriv civic location specifications (RFC 4776 and RFC 5139) define XML and binary (DHCP) forms for civic addresses. Since then, new use cases have appeared. Some long-standing national address formats do not fit the existing elements, and the RFC says that creating a new element is better than overloading an existing field, which may cause confusion.

The XML format already allows extra elements. The DHCP format has no such facility. A recipient can only ignore elements it does not understand, so anything unknown is discarded when it converts from one format to the other. A converter would have to understand every extension to keep it.

The additions are backward compatible: old implementations may lose extension information, but extensions do not affect an implementation that conforms to RFC 4776 or RFC 5139.
sections.eli5: If you copy a form onto a new sheet and do not know what a box means, you might skip it. Then the information is lost. This RFC makes sure the boxes can be copied across even by someone who does not understand them.

sections.title: Defining Extensions in XML
sections.content:
The civic schema in RFC 5139 is an ordered list of elements with an extension point at the end. New elements are defined in a new XML namespace, whether they are meant for private, local or global use. They SHOULD use the basic caType schema type, which has an optional xml:lang attribute.

The RFC's example is a fictitious canals authority that adds a bridge element in its own namespace and writes <cdc:bridge> after the standard elements. A receiver that does not know the element can still use the rest of the address, and can pass the whole address on, for example to a LoST server, unchanged.

New extensions MUST be defined only for the XML format. Further extensions to the DHCP format itself are prohibited, because they could not be conveyed safely where conversion is possible.
sections.eli5: Each new address line gets its own labelled stamp showing who invented it. Programs that do not know the stamp can still read the rest of the address.

sections.title: The Extension CAtype in DHCP
sections.content:
To carry an XML extension in DHCP, the RFC defines the extension CAtype, CAtype code 40. Its value holds three things separated by single space characters: the namespace URI, the local name of the XML element, and the element's text content.

The Length field counts the octets of those three parts, including the two spaces. The content is UTF-8 text with a maximum of 255 octets, so a long namespace URI and name leave less room for the value.

This only works for elements with textual content and an optional xml:lang attribute. Elements with complex content or other attributes (other than namespace bindings) MUST be ignored if they are not understood.

When converting back to XML, the converter chooses the namespace prefix. The namespace URI in DHCP is written as a URL, but it should not be dereferenced; doing so serves no useful purpose.
sections.eli5: It is like putting a label on a parcel that says who made it, what it is and what is inside, all on one line. Anyone can repack it without opening it.

sections.title: A Conversion Example
sections.content:
The RFC converts an XML address with two extension namespaces: a post namespace with lamp and pylon elements, and an ap airport namespace with airport, terminal, concourse and gate elements. Standard elements become ordinary CAtypes (for example CAtype[1] = CA), and each extension becomes its own CAtype 40 entry.

The converter did not need to know anything about posts or airports. It only copied the namespace, name and value.
sections.eli5: The extra lines each get copied onto the new form word for word, with their sender's label, even though the copier has never heard of lamp posts or gates.

sections.title: The Four New Elements
sections.content:
The RFC uses its own method to define four elements in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:geopriv10:civicAddr:ext, and says they also serve as a template for future extensions.

  • Pole number (PN): the unique identifier carried by utility and lamp posts in some areas. In some countries the label also carries the local emergency number, such as 110.
  • Milepost (MP): a post showing a mile or kilometer distance along a road, trail or railroad right of way.
  • Street type prefix (STP): allows "123 Boulevard Colorado" as well as "123 Colorado Boulevard".
  • House number prefix (HNP): allows "Z123 Main Street", complementing the existing house number suffix that allows "123A Main Street".

All four are declared with the caType type in an XML schema, which the RFC registers.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds four new address lines: the number on a lamp post, the number on a road marker, a street word before the street name, and a letter before the house number.

sections.title: Extensions and LoST Validation
sections.content:
The Location-to-Service Translation protocol (LoST, RFC 5222) is used for emergency call routing and can also validate a location. A validation response returns a <locationValidation> element with lists of valid, invalid and unchecked civic elements.

The RelaxNG schema in RFC 5222 requires the names in these lists to be namespace qualified, which makes the example in RFC 5222 erroneous. This document normatively updates RFC 5222: every element listed in <valid>, <invalid> or <unchecked> MUST be qualified with a namespace. For example, country A1 becomes ca:country ca:A1, and extension elements appear as cae:PN and so on. The LoST schema itself does not change.
sections.eli5: When a list names address lines, each name must say whose rulebook it comes from, so two lines with the same name from different makers cannot be mixed up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that no security threats are directly introduced. People who create new civic extensions should read Sections 4.3.1 and 5.1 of RFC 3694 to understand the environments where the elements will be used, and new elements should be registered only if the registrant understands the associated risks. The threats that apply to the DHCP and XML civic formats are described in RFC 4776 and RFC 5139.
sections.eli5: Adding a new address line is not dangerous by itself. People who invent new lines should think about who will read them and what could go wrong.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA allocated CAtype code 40 for the extension CAtype. The CAtypes registry is closed to new numeric CAtypes except by IESG Approval under unusual circumstances, so new registrations use code 40 with a template: namespace URI, local name, description, contact and a Type, plus optional example, specification and schema.

The registry also loses its "NENA" column, renames "PIDF" to "Local Name" and gains "Namespace URI", "Contact", "Schema" and "Type" columns. Type A elements are intended for wide use and SHOULD be implemented by clients, and need IETF Review. Type B elements MAY be implemented and need Expert Review. Registrations that are close to an existing element SHOULD explain why the existing one was not reused.

The four new elements are registered as Type A, and IANA also registered the namespace and the schema.
sections.eli5: There is a public list of known address lines. Popular lines need a careful vote to be added, and less common ones only need an expert to look them over.

data.title: Extension elements become CAtype 40 entries
data.code:
<post:lamp>2471</post:lamp>
<ap:gate>36B</ap:gate>

becomes

CAtype[40]  = http://postsoftheworld.example.com/ns lamp 2471
CAtype[40]  = http://example.com/airport/5.0 gate 36B

viz.caption: THE FOUR ELEMENTS DEFINED IN RFC 6848

cells: Identifier on a lamp post or utility pole
Distance marker along a road, trail or railroad
Street type before the name, as in 123 Boulevard Colorado
Prefix before the house number, as in Z123 Main Street
